title: Sports AI: A Game-Changing Partner For Coaches
text:
With the rise of data analytics and artificial intelligence in sports, concerns have been raised about their potential to replace coaches' intuition and creativity. AlphaPlay is proving that AI can be a valuable partner for coaches, enhancing their strategies and decision-making process rather than replacing them. In effect, AlphaPlay empowers coaches to focus on the human aspects of the game.
By sifting through massive datasets and delivering actionable information in clear language, AlphaPlay helps teams identify opponent weaknesses, optimize player development, and unearth hidden talent—all while saving valuable time and resources.
Ultimately, AI becomes a highly productive assistant coach for teams, rather than a replacement for human expertise. It epitomizes the symbiotic relationship between technology and human expertise in sports.
AlphaPlay AI: Elevating Pre-Match Strategies And Talent Acquisition
The global sports AI market is projected to boom, reaching nearly $21 billion by 2029 (Mordor Intelligence). AI tools like AlphaPlay are leading the charge.
While coaches use analytics, all the time, AI offers two distinct benefits. First, it analyzes a significantly larger pool of data. Second, it delivers insights in clear, actionable language, boosting coach confidence in split-second decisions. Importantly, coaches retain control, strategically using AI-generated advice rather than blindly following it.
AlphaPlay—led by data- and user experience-focused CEO Alice Wang and her husband sports AI expert Brian Hall, founder and head of AI—was developed in 2022 for baseball. It has proven even more effective in complex team sports like hockey, football, and soccer.
The platform was unveiled at the 2023 MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference. The conference brings together industry professionals and students to explore cutting-edge trends in analytics and business, fostering innovation and advancing accessibility and representation across the global sports landscape. AlphaPlay quickly secured beta clients in hockey and soccer. These partnerships fueled the development of the pre-match suite and key player identification products.
At the 2024 conference, AlphaPlay secured paying clients across the U.S., South America, and Europe. AlphaPlay analyzes vast datasets to uncover hidden patterns and generate actionable insights. It empowers coaches to optimize player development, identify talent, and exploit opponents' offensive and defensive weaknesses. These insights are delivered in clear, everyday language, fostering informed human decision-making.
"AI is an equalizer," says Wang. “Women’s sports and minor league teams don't have the budget for data scientists infrastructure and paying all kinds of analysts.” Limited-budget teams can now compete by leveraging AlphaPlay's affordable, easy-to-understand reports, which are translated into the local language.
Compared to traditional video review, AlphaPlay streamlines pre-game preparation, pinpointing critical mismatches in moments and delivering insights tailored to each team's specific opponent and playing philosophy.
"AI impacts football by automating the data journey from extraction to implementation, boosting work-hour efficiency for data staff,” Rodrigo Picchioni, head of analytics at Atletico Mineiro, Brazilian Soccer League. “Additionally, its user-friendly interfaces—together with generative AI features—empower non-data-literate users to explore and utilize complex data points effortlessly."
Professional teams typically play at least one game a week, sometimes two. Coaches and players are under enormous pressure to prepare, whether it is to drill, change their tactics, or enhance certain parts of their play, depending on who they're playing.
"AlphaPlay has proven to be valuable and is becoming an indispensable tool within our analytics department,” Alejandro Dávila, Director of Analysis at Mazatlán FC in Liga MX, Mexican Soccer League. “From dissecting opposition strategies to streamlining our scouting efforts, AlphaPlay demonstrates how generative AI can produce more insights in far less time."
“Some teams are highly aggressive, others play defensively, and sometimes that philosophy changes depending on how they're playing in the season,” said Wang. “Everything is customized to the team.” And the reports are in the team’s language.
Sports are ideal for analysis using AI. The outcomes are clear-cut, games have a beginning and end, and the rules are consistent. “They're very few industries, where everybody plays by the rules in the same way that sports does,” said Wang.
Sports AI: Partner, Not Replacement, for Coaches
Coaches often have concerns that AI might stifle their experience-based decision-making, intuition, and strategic creativity by prioritizing cold data over intangibles. At the first meeting, AlphaPlay demonstrates how it empowers—not replaces—coaches and players. Wang brings a report that shows how AlphaPlay saves them valuable time by identifying opponent vulnerabilities, allowing them to focus on strategy and game preparation.
When introducing AlphaPlay, Wang shows teams how AI is a powerful tool that complements human expertise. Coaches leverage AI-generated insights to analyze passing and defensive networks, pinpointing vulnerabilities in opponent formations. This type of analysis, typically requiring hours of video review by coaches, is done on the platform in seconds.
A good example of how AI augments coaches is if a team must replace a player with a specific skill set within a set budget. AlphaPlay identifies potential player replacements that scouts may be unaware of. This is an "aha moment," showcasing AI's ability to unearth hidden gems. Coaches still add in factors like team dynamics and other intangibles before a decision is made.
The data explosion in sports, including video analysis, overwhelms human analysts as they search for actionable insights. AI, like AlphaPlay, excels at sifting through massive datasets, identifying patterns, and generating valuable information that coaches might miss or don’t have time to do before the next game. AlphaPlay simplifies the processes and analyses that coaches have done all along. It provides the framework for informed decision-making, not the final call.
"We've done the hard work of interpreting data," says Wang. AlphaPlay becomes a highly productive assistant coach, freeing coaches to focus on the human elements of the game.

title: This $2.2 Billion Startup’s GPT-4 Powered AI Bot Demystifies Health Insurance
text:
Livongo cofounder Glen Tullman has promised his latest startup Transcarent will use AI to help people navigate and pay for healthcare services, but it may be just another Band-aid for America’s growing $4.5 trillion healthcare bill.
By Katie Jennings, Forbes Staff
Glen Tullman believes telehealth, as we know it, is dead. The future, according to the venture capital investor and serial entrepreneur, is not video-based but text-based. “All of the virtual care we're doing now is all going to move to chat,” he told Forbes, estimating that in three years 80 to 85% of all telehealth interactions you have with your doctor will be written.
It’s a bold prediction from the same man who sold his last company Livongo, which made managing diabetes care easier, to telehealth giant Teladoc for $18.5 billion at the dizzying market highs of 2020. As of Tuesday’s close, Teladoc had a market cap of $2.2 billion, which Tullman blamed on “poor leadership” and a high-cost, labor intensive structure due to the demand of staffing video visits. Text-based care and insights, with help from the latest advances in generative artificial intelligence, will cause a “titanic shift,” he said.
Now, he’s teasing a new AI chatbot built on the same technology that powers ChatGPT, as part of his latest venture Transcarent, which announced a $126 million Series D at a $2.2 billion valuation earlier this month. The bot will aim to answer the health insurance-related questions that regularly stump more than half of Americans, like: How much will I have to pay for this doctor’s visit? What’s my deductible? Can you help me find a doctor? It’s part of Transcarent’s goal of becoming a one-stop shop to help average Americans navigate the opaque and oftentimes infuriating $4.5 trillion U.S. healthcare system.
Transcarent, which offers an app with 24/7 chat-based primary care services, lower cost drug options, referrals and second opinions, has raised $450 million since its founding in 2020 from investors including Tullman’s firm 7wire Ventures and General Catalyst. It also works directly with health systems to get better rates for major health events like surgeries and cancer care.
But experts say Transcarent’s business may be more of a Band-aid than a panacea, even though there is a growing market – Grand View Research estimates it at $10 billion – to help people navigate how to find and pay for healthcare services. The only reason this opportunity exists is due to the dysfunction of the U.S. healthcare system, Ge Bai, a healthcare accounting and policy professor at Johns Hopkins University, told Forbes. “It exploits a structural weakness of the current healthcare system, which is extreme complexity and the information disadvantage of patients,” said Bai. Navigation services are more of a “tweak” than a “fundamental change,” she added, but there’s so much waste in the system that “even a small tweak can still make a difference.”
Most healthcare navigation services depend heavily on human call centers, which have high labor costs. That’s where Tullman sees the greatest potential for his new AI tool: to cut the cost in half. The bot is currently built on top of OpenAI’s GPT-4 large language model, and includes in-house specialized models that can determine if a user has asked a medical question or is experiencing an emergency, at which point a human needs to take over.
Tullman said companies are currently paying $10 to $15 per employee per month for human-based navigation services, while he plans to offer them for $5. “This is truly a generational step,” said Tullman. “We've gone from boring navigation, which wasn't really interesting, to one place to get all of your care.” Transcarent will start offering the tool to its customers in January 2025.
Those customers are largely employers, as Transcarent is targeting a specific type of health insurance: self-funded plans. Around 134 million Americans receive health insurance benefits through their employer in an arrangement where the employer is on the hook for its workers’ total healthcare costs, according to 2021 estimates from the Department of Labor (the latest data available). Those costs have been steadily going up, rising 7% to $8,435 in yearly premiums for a single worker in 2023, according to the health policy research organization KFF. These ever-rising costs have spawned an entire industry dedicated to helping employers lower their total spending by hand-holding employees through their healthcare options.
“This market is a bit niche right now,” Chris Whaley, a health policy professor at Brown University told Forbes. “But as healthcare costs are just continuing to grow, and many employers are facing inflationary pressures, that will most likely really start to expand.”
In trying to crack this market, Tullman is facing off against a mix of startups, such as Carrum Health and Included Health, and incumbents, like Quantum Health and publicly-traded Accolade Health, which had $360 million in 2023 revenues and a $577 million market cap at Tuesday’s close. In the fourth quarter, Accolade was also EBITDA positive for the first time — a good measure of the company’s core operating profitability, even though it had a $7.5 million loss for the year, said Bai. Tullman said Transcarent is not yet profitable and was “approaching” $100 million in revenue run rate at the end of 2023.
“This is all kind of background noise until somebody has an event that triggers a need to get help navigating the healthcare system.”
This new health benefits bot builds on Transcarent’s experience using an AI bot that helps its doctors with patient intakes, which it purchased from health AI startup 98point6 in 2023 for $100 million. Along with the bot, Transcarent also obtained 98point6’s doctor group and employer customers as well as what Tullman called a “golden asset” not yet publicly disclosed: 1 million patient-doctor chat conversations over five years. That data is now being used to validate and do safety testing for the new tool.
When Forbes demoed a prototype of the AI tool, the chatbot was able to determine when a person was seeking medical advice. Asked a question about shoulder pain, the bot recommended speaking to a virtual physical therapist or having an orthopedic consult. For a question about suicidal thoughts, it also recommended speaking to a person. Ben Nguyen, a doctor and Transcarent’s lead product manager, said that if the bot was asked anything about self-harm in a real situation, that chat would be immediately escalated to a human.
It also successfully answered simple questions about health insurance, like how much money was left before hitting the deductible and how much an in-network primary care visit might cost. But it struggled with some complex questions, flubbing when asked to find a Spanish-speaking orthopedic surgeon in the Bay Area, instead recommending a psychiatrist. (However, it was able to correctly recommend a Spanish-speaking endocrinologist in the Bay Area.)
Competitors could just spin up their own GPT-4-based versions of the same type of chatbot, but Tullman isn’t worried about copycats. While there may be a general perception that building AI tools with foundation models is fast and cheap, he said it’s still pricey. From the compute power to all of the training and validation that was needed for the bot to work well and safely for customers, building a similar bot would still cost millions, which Tullman is betting will be too high of a barrier for competitors.
Even if the bot functions technically well, there is still a major hurdle: will employees actually use it? Healthcare consulting firm Mercer, a division of MarshMcLennan, estimates that 46% of companies with 20,000 or more employees already offer some form of advocacy or navigation solutions to their employees, but uptake is hugely variable from company-to-company. “One of the age-old challenges is none of this really matters until it really matters,” said Jonathan Pas, a partner at MercerWELL. “This is all kind of background noise until somebody has an event that triggers a need to get help navigating the healthcare system.”
Transcarent customer Pilot Flying J, the gas and convenience store chain acquired by Berkshire Hathaway earlier this year, told Forbes around 53% percent of the 19,000 eligible employees and dependents on the company’s health plan have downloaded the Transcarent app and 77% of those are active users. Diana Morgan, Pilot’s director of benefits and well-being, believes that’s partly motivated by the premium discount Pilot offers for people who sign-up, but it’s also about giving people “more power to understand what's happening with their health.”
For Tullman, it’s all about making that experience as frictionless as possible, similar to his Livongo playbook. He didn’t invent blood glucose monitoring – he acquired the hardware and made it much easier for diabetics to manage their insulin levels, and combined it with perks like free testing strips. With Transcarent, he has similarly been buying other companies to assemble the necessary pieces to make things seamless for patients. “This is creating Amazon for healthcare,” he said. “It's one place to get all of your care.”

title: Council Post: Into The Deep: How Businesses And Consumers Can Stay Vigilant In The Deep Fakes Era
text:
I am the CEO of NovelVox, an AI-enabled contact center solution provider. I help organizations deliver impeccable customer experience.
Seeing is no longer believing.
The other day I saw a video titled “This Is Not Morgan Freeman,” wherein "Morgan Freeman" talks about how he is not Morgan Freeman. He goes on to say that he is not even a human being. Given the similarity to Freeman’s calm and collected demeanor and his signature raspy voice, it is hard to believe that he is not real. The amount of detail in the video that suggests him being the real deal is uncanny. Yet, in the video, he communicates against the idea of his existence.
This was nothing short of flabbergasting. The video was shared by a Dutch deep fake YouTube channel Diep Nep in 2021.
Three years later, AI has only gotten more powerful. The recent developments in generative AI prove that AI is clearly strong enough to make people say things they would never say and do things they would never do.
These developments call for us to be more vigilant in trusting what we see on the internet. Even more so if you are running a business, as customer privacy is a major concern in the ever-changing world of AI.
But how does one go about safeguarding customer trust in this increasingly "infocalpytic" era of AI? To understand, let’s first look at what a deep fake is and its impending danger to society.
What is a deep fake?
A deep fake refers to a piece of synthetic media created with the help of AI wherein a person in the image or video is swapped with an artificially made person and made to do or say often transgressive things. It involves the manipulation of audio, images or videos to create content that appears authentic but is not.
The term "deep fake" comes from "deep learning" (a subset of machine learning) and "fake." Deep learning algorithms analyze vast amounts of data to learn patterns and features, allowing them to generate highly realistic imitations of human speech, facial expressions and movements.
How is a deep fake created?
To create a deep fake, a neural network is trained on a large dataset of images or videos of a target person. Once trained, the algorithm can generate new content by synthesizing the target person's likeness onto another person's body or altering their voice.
A 2022 Forbes article, "Overview Of How To Create Deepfakes—It’s Scarily Simple," breaks down the procedure for easier understanding.
What is the impact of deep fakes on businesses and consumers?
Deepfakes, primarily crafted to deceive viewers by presenting false information as authentic, constitute a significant risk to companies and organizations. This threat arises from viewers' challenges in discerning genuine content from fabricated material.
Let me share a story of a cybercrime to elucidate my point. In 2019, The Wall Street Journal published an article that explained the case of cybercrime conducted with the help of AI: “The criminals used artificial intelligence-based software to impersonate a chief executive’s voice and demand a fraudulent transfer of €220,000 ($243,000).”
The CEO of the U.K.-based energy firm, the article explains, thought he was talking with his boss, the chief executive of the company’s German parent company. The fraudster asked the CEO to transfer the funds to a Hungarian supplier. The CEO, recognizing the “boss’ slight German accent and the melody of his voice on the phone” complied immediately.
This is only a small example of how AI manipulation can harm companies and consumers alike. For instance, Pindrop, one of my company's partners, has identified four ways attackers are using deep fakes to attack contact centers:
1. The use of synthetic voice to bypass interactive voice response (IVR).
2. The use of synthetic voice to request profile change with agents.
3. Training voice bots to mimic IVRs.
4. The use of synthetic voice to navigate IVR and steal basic account details.
How can you identify deep fakes and stay vigilant?
As AI continues to evolve, these challenges bring up serious concerns for both consumers and businesses. But it’s not the end of the world.
Despite such rapid development and virtually an endless pit of data, AI has still not been able to capture the nuances of human beings. And it will be a long time before it does. This is where the solution to the deep fake cataclysm lies. To begin understanding how to solve this challenge, here are a few ways to identify a deep fake:
• Pay attention to the face. As mentioned earlier, AI is yet to completely replicate human features, which can show in minute details of facial features such as the mouth, creases on the forehead, breakouts and uneven tonality.
• The eyes don’t lie. Another human feature that AI has a hard time mastering is the eyes. AI often messes up the eyes, mixing up light and shadow and their placements. Moreover, the way a person blinks in an AI-created video is often a giveaway.
• Focus on the background. Deep fake videos are often blurry with minimal to no details in the background, making up for a somewhat awkward composition. Pay attention to where you usually don’t pay attention to, and you might identify an AI-generated video.
Besides these proactive measures, the deep fake challenge also needs to be addressed on a broader level. For instance, identifying deep fake audio is not the same as identifying Deep Fake videos. Deep fake audio detection requires a multifaceted strategy that involves knowledge, technology and alertness.
Some of the steps companies can take to tackle the deep fake challenge are setting up stringent legislative and regulatory models, introducing corporate policies and voluntary action, investing in employee education and training as well as in anti-deep fake technology that includes deep fake detection, content authentication and deep fake prevention.

title: Council Post: Beyond Buzzwords: AI's Practical Impact On Supply Chain Operations
text:
Richard is the CEO of LeanDNA, a purpose-built analytics platform for factory inventory optimization.
In today's hyperconnected world, supply chain management (SCM) stands at the forefront of complexity and innovation. Traditional methods struggle to keep pace with the demands of modern business, where agility, precision and foresight are paramount. Fortunately, as manufacturing organizations grapple with these challenges, a beacon of innovation emerges in the form of artificial intelligence (AI). AI is poised to revolutionize supply chain operations and transform the role of supply chain teams for the future.
The pressure on supply chain executives to navigate disruptions while maintaining optimal inventory levels is palpable and intensifying. According to insights from a supply chain readiness survey conducted by Wakefield Research and our comapny, a staggering 96% of supply chain executives say they face pressure to balance preparedness for major disruption with avoiding excess inventory. This underscores the urgent need for adaptive strategies and technological solutions that provide real-time insights and enable agile decision-making.
While many organizations have embarked on digital transformations and are investing in advanced technologies, a significant gap remains. Despite these investments, a whopping 76% of organizations lack a predictive view of supply and demand. This gap hinders strategic planning and limits the ability to anticipate and mitigate potential disruptions.
One of the primary challenges supply chain professionals face is the pervasive reliance on manual data handling. Despite technological advancements, supply chain teams spend an average of 35% of their time on manual data manipulation. This slows down processes and increases the likelihood of errors and inefficiencies. Moreover, with over nine in ten executives admitting to relying on gut instinct for decision-making at least some of the time, the need for data-driven predictive guidance becomes increasingly evident.
Enter AI—a transformative force poised to revolutionize supply chain operations by harnessing the power of data and analytics. By leveraging AI algorithms and machine learning, organizations can unlock unprecedented visibility, efficiency, and agility across their supply chains. From inventory optimization to critical shortage prioritization, AI enables organizations to make smarter decisions faster, thereby gaining a competitive advantage in a volatile marketplace. A recent Harvard Business Review article goes into further detail on how machine learning will transform supply chain management.
However, to fully realize the promise of AI in supply chain management, we must move beyond the buzzwords and delve into the "why" and "how" of AI implementation. There's an urgent need for organizations to evolve their approach, focusing not just on adopting AI technologies but on understanding where and how AI can truly drive value in the market. Dispelling the mystique behind the buzzword, we must emphasize practical applications and tangible benefits that AI can bring to supply chain operations.
Moreover, connecting the survey results to the promise of AI reveals a clear path forward. By addressing the gaps identified—such as the lack of predictive views and overreliance on manual data handling—organizations can leverage AI to bridge these deficiencies and drive tangible outcomes. Whether it's optimizing inventory levels, prioritizing critical shortages or streamlining decision-making processes, AI offers a myriad of opportunities for supply chain transformation.
The impact of AI goes beyond just optimizing existing processes; it will fundamentally transform the role of supply chain teams. In the AI-enabled supply chain of the future, human workers become strategic orchestrators, leveraging AI-driven insights to anticipate issues impacting production readiness, identify opportunities and proactively initiate prioritized actions to optimize supply chain execution. By augmenting human intelligence with machine learning capabilities, organizations can unlock new levels of productivity, efficiency and supply chain resilience.
However, the journey towards AI-driven supply chain excellence is not without its challenges. One significant hurdle is the issue of change management. As organizations seek to adopt AI technologies and transform their supply chain operations, they must navigate a myriad of cultural, organizational, and technical barriers.
To overcome these challenges, organizations must adopt change management strategies that foster a culture of innovation, collaboration and continuous learning. This includes clear communication about the benefits of AI adoption to your supply chain teams, providing adequate training and support for employees, and creating a supportive environment that encourages experimentation and risk-taking. By addressing these challenges head-on, manufacturing organizations can accelerate their journey toward AI-driven supply chain excellence and unlock new opportunities for growth and success.
Developing a comprehensive implementation roadmap is essential for successful AI integration. This roadmap should encompass several key components:
- Assessment and planning: Begin by assessing the current state of the supply chain and identifying areas within your organization where AI can drive the most significant impact. Common areas of opportunity are action prioritization and confidence scoring with automated execution.
- Technology infrastructure: Ensure that the necessary infrastructure is in place to support AI implementation.
- Data quality: Establish robust data management processes to ensure quality, reliability and security of supply chain data. This may include data cleansing, normalization and integration efforts to create a unified data environment for AI analysis.
- Training and skills development: Provide comprehensive training programs to equip supply chain teams with the skills and knowledge needed to leverage AI effectively in their daily workflow. This may involve both technical training on AI tools and platforms as well as soft skills development in areas such as data interpretation and decision-making.
- Scaling with user-based workflows: Once proven successful, scale AI initiatives across the supply chain and integrate them into day-to-day operations with purpose-built workflows for key roles such as production planners, material buyers and suppliers.
The future of supply chain management is AI-driven, and you need to prepare your teams for these newly emerging roles. As organizations embrace AI technologies and empower their teams with data-driven insights, they will unlock new opportunities for innovation and growth. The journey toward intelligent supply chain execution is underway, and organizations that innovate and harness the power of AI will emerge as leaders in the new era of supply chain management. With a comprehensive implementation roadmap and a commitment to change management, organizations can navigate the AI revolution and drive transformative change across their supply chain teams.

title: Council Post: How AI Is Ushering In The Age Of Intelligent DevOps
text:
Sanjay Gidwani is Chief Operating Officer for Copado, a leading DevOps and testing platform for enterprise SaaS deployments.
Every day, you see the latest story on how AI is changing the world. In fact, no other technology has made a greater impact in such a short period of time. In software development, we've seen several companies introduce AI copilots to assist developers with code creation, but AI is expected to have a more far-reaching impact on DevOps.
I believe that AI is set to transform traditional DevOps into intelligent DevOps, which would impact the entire software development life cycle. The evolution is already underway with the initial introduction of copilots and we can expect more AI-driven changes to come on the scene at a rapid pace.
The key function in DevOps is usually referred to as continuous integration (CI) and continuous delivery (CD). It can sound like everything is automated and happens without human intervention, but the reality doesn't live up to the promise of the name. Most enterprises have done a good job with the CI part, making it easy for many developers to integrate their work. This is usually referred to in DevOps as the “build” phase. AI copilots have already begun helping developers in the build phase, writing code for them and auto-completing their work.
The CD phase still isn't there yet. It’s a much more difficult task that requires greater automation. In fact, the word "continuous" doesn't make much sense for most businesses. Business-to-consumer companies like Netflix and Google adopted CD to deliver small changes to users as soon as they were ready. For most large companies, there are regulatory and compliance issues to deal with that slow down delivery. Then, there is the issue that business users can only absorb so much change in the way they do their jobs. This is why most IT organizations release changes once per month, once per quarter or twice each year.
Intelligent DevOps could allow businesses to increase automation for improved efficiency but within the framework of compliance, security and quality that regulated companies require and at a pace that fits with the ability of the business to absorb the change. Rather than focus on going fast, it’s about doing more with less while obeying the regulatory speed limits.
The next generation of AI tools is expected to address two vital aspects of intelligent DevOps: planning and testing. Intelligent DevOps could help teams in the planning phase ensure that they're working on the right thing, that everyone is on the same page with respect to goals and that all of the impacts have been analyzed so the estimate of the development effort is more accurate. If the C-suite signs off on a million-dollar project, it needs to come in on time and on budget.
Testing is often overlooked regarding its impact on DevOps. Intelligent DevOps recognizes that testing is an integral part of the process and not a separate activity bolted on at the end of development. It could make it possible for subject matter experts to play a larger role in the planning and testing phases and reduce the need for expensive test developers. Generative AI can help with enriching requirements and writing the actual tests to ensure proper functionality, known as test-driven development.
As noted above, the continuous delivery phase relies on handcrafted scripts, resulting in a system that's unable to quickly change with shifting business needs. Intelligent DevOps enables compliance, IT operations and the business to set priorities in a declarative manner with the underlying AI-driven platform to move changes through the system according to the needs of the business while still obeying all of the rules set by industry-specific regulations.
Benefits of intelligent DevOps include cost reduction and improved productivity. Everyone wants to do more with less. Sometimes, this is due to budget constraints, but often, you just can’t hire enough people with the right skills. There are many articles on the productivity boost that generative AI can provide for code development. This is part of intelligent DevOps, and those benefits still accrue. These same technologies can be applied to test generation and requirements analysis, which enable business analysts and quality teams to improve efficiency and productivity.
Huge costs can also be incurred when defects make it to production, especially if there's associated downtime or security breaches. Intelligent DevOps could significantly reduce these defects by identifying them earlier in the process.
Finally, by delivering more change through the process in less time, DevOps teams can generate ideas for improvement and quickly deliver that change to production. These ideas can also positively impact costs by making employees more efficient, and some can boost top-line revenue by improving lead conversion and close rates.
For years now, the proponents of DevOps have promised some of the same benefits highlighted above, but the reality has fallen short of expectations. DevOps requires people, processes and technology to work in harmony to achieve results. The previous state-of-the-art technology required people to be experts in DevOps practices and follow a process that was, at times, quite demanding. Intelligent DevOps is expected to deliver on the original promise by reducing the skills required to realize the full benefits while allowing teams to focus on the jobs they were hired to do.

title: Council Post: Harmonies Beyond Boundaries: Music, Technology And Human Connection
text:
Susan Erwin Prowse, Co-Founder/ Co-Owner, Big Red Dog Productions, International Touring Artist.
Propelled by augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR) and artificial intelligence (AI), I believe the music industry is on the brink of transformation. The global pandemic only accelerated this shift, moving the industry from traditional venues to digital platforms that may soon become the main stage for artistic expression.
This evolution in how we experience music, while seen by some as a temporary adaptation, may very well be a preview of a digitally-integrated future.
Impact Of The Pandemic On Music
The swift move to virtual platforms during the pandemic demonstrated the music industry's adaptability and resilience. Artists and producers embraced a digital-first approach, navigating challenges and innovating on the fly.
This era was defined by an explosion of virtual concerts, connecting artists from their homes to a global audience through screens, creating new forms of audience engagement that have the potential to persist beyond the crisis.
Role Of AI In Music
As a fervent explorer of AI, I've seen its profound impact on music, reshaping everything from creation to consumption. AI is not just altering the music landscape—it's expanding it with new interactive experiences. For those in the industry, here are some potentials of the technology when it comes to live shows.
• Virtual reality concerts. Fans can attend 3D concerts via VR headsets, choose viewpoints and interact with digital merchandising or artist avatars.
• Interactive setlists. AI could tailor setlists in real-time based on audience mood, enhancing engagement.
• Augmented reality shows. AR could be used by fans to view synchronized visuals or artist trivia on their mobile devices during performances.
• Direct artist interaction. Based on traditional meet-and-greets, fans could communicate with artist avatars for personalized interaction during or post-show.
• Customizable venues. With new technologies, audiences can customize their concert environment, adjusting visual settings or selecting themed backdrops.
• Gamification. Interactive games can also be integrated into concerts, rewarding fan participation with points and perks.
• Emotional engagement. AI can adjust the music and visuals in response to real-time emotional feedback from the audience.
Vision For The Future
The convergence of AR, VR and AI promises a seamless blend of physical and virtual realities in music. Future concerts could offer performances tailored to personal environments, with augmented overlays that create the illusion of artists performing live in your space.
Pushback And Ethical Implications
However, embracing these technologies also introduces ethical considerations, including the authenticity of creative expression and the potential displacement of traditional musical skills. We're on a trajectory to integrate AI deeply into our lives, and it's critical to navigate this path thoughtfully to maintain the creative soul of music. The risk of obsolescence looms for those who ignore these evolving tools and fail to be a part of their integration.
Elevating Live Performances With Metaverse And AR Technologies
Like with AI, integrating live performances within the metaverse using AR technologies has the potential to dramatically enhance both physical and virtual concerts. Based on examples like Coachella, which partnered with Fortnite to create a virtual stage to align with its festival, here are some potential uses I foresee for these technologies.
• AR-enhanced stages. Imagine AR transforming physical stages into dynamic, interactive platforms that react to the music.
• Virtual concert customization. In the metaverse, fans might choose exotic virtual locales for their concert experience—from serene beaches to dramatic mountains.
• Interactive physical venues. AR could allow audiences in physical venues to interact with the show through their devices, influencing everything from lighting to setlists in real time.
Conclusion
As the music industry continues to evolve, integrating AR, VR and AI can not only enhance an audience's sensory and emotional engagement but also pioneer new realms of accessibility and artistic expression. The path forward will require us to balance these technologies with the intrinsic human touch at the heart of music, ensuring it continues to resonate deeply and universally.

title: Exclusive: New Gong CMO Emily He On Her Move From Microsoft
text:
After more than two years as Microsoft’s corporate vice president for business applications marketing, Emily He will be Gong’s new chief marketing officer. He worked to build the strategy and drive growth for Microsoft’s Copilot platform for business functions. Gong, a revenue intelligence platform that derives its insight from customer interactions, has used AI since its inception. He gave an exclusive interview to Forbes about her new job and how AI is changing what a CMO does.
This conversation has been edited for length, continuity and clarity. An excerpt was in Wednesday’s Forbes CMO newsletter.
Why are you moving from Microsoft to Gong?
He: In the last few years, I’ve been at Microsoft leading business applications, so my responsibility is to sell and market all the software targeting line-of-business buyers, whether it’s sales, marketing, service, supply chain, finance or IT. As you know, Microsoft has been going super super hard on marketing AI. In the last few years, we’ve really used AI to transform the way [things] across these business functions work, including sales, marketing, services, et cetera. We’ve been launching Copilot for Sales, Copilot for Service and Copilot for Finance, and there’s more products to come.
I really see the Gong journey as an extension of what I’ve already done at Microsoft. What I really admire about Gong is Gong is very clear on the target buyer, and Gong has a deep expertise and understanding in what the revenue teams need. Gong has been incorporating AI in its solution since day one. Gong has a really impressive value proposition when it comes to addressing the needs for the revenue teams, whether it is understanding customers or coming up with deal strategies. I am excited about the ability to go deeper into addressing the revenue team’s requirements. I think Gong is one of the most exciting companies right now in the AI era.
You’ve been central to Microsoft’s strategy with Copilot and extending it to different use applications. What, specifically, will you bring to Gong to help the company move forward?
At Microsoft, we’ve been on the Copilot journey for the last year to year and a half. All the lessons I’ve learned, I will bring to Gong.
When it comes to AI, I think we’ve gone beyond hype. Now, customers are really asking for tangible business outcomes and business benefits. Gong already has a wealth of customers, and Gong has already demonstrated quantifiable business benefits. I’m going to work with the Gong team to better articulate the value proposition and business benefits we can bring to customers.
When it comes to AI, I think we went from being excited about a new technology to being more practical. The questions customers are asking about are: ‘How do I deploy AI?’ ‘What buying criteria should I be using when I evaluate AI technology?’ and ‘How do I deal with change management to bring technology to users?’ I think Gong has an opportunity to bring a lot more practical guidance to customers and really guide them through the entire AI purchasing and deployment journey.
Everybody is looking for customer stories. When you buy new technology, you always want to know someone in the same industry who has done it. You want to learn from their journey. The great thing is, Gong has more than 4,000 customers, so we have a lot of customer stories to tell. We’re going to put a lot of focus on telling customer stories.
A lot of companies right now are doing what I call ‘AI washing.’ They have ‘AI’ in every single product name and in their marketing messages, but they actually don't have the product truth behind it. Gong is the opposite of that. Gong, from day one, was incorporating AI in its solutions, but at the time customers weren’t ready to embrace AI, so Gong was a little bit shy about touting its AI capabilities. Now is the complete opposite. Customers are ready for AI. They want to hear more about AI, and I think Gong has a great opportunity to clearly articulate its key differentiation when it comes to AI: Proprietary AI models and the AI foundation.
Just five years ago, before AI was in everything and widely used, how much pressure were CMOs under to deliver? How has that changed since AI has become a more prevalent tool?
The C-suite is under tremendous pressure across all their business functions, whether it’s sales, service or marketing. CMOs are no exception. CMOs are under pressure to come up with the right solution to embrace AI in their marketing practices. CMOs have the dual responsibility: Number one, help articulate how the company as a whole is embracing AI across all the business functions. The second thing is: How are you using AI in your marketing data to better deliver campaigns or messaging?
I see a lot of CMOs embracing AI in content generation, or generating videos, transforming the way they do their creatives and messaging. But I think the more important thing, and this is where Gong comes to play, is to use customer interaction data to gain a better understanding of the customers, and then craft your messaging accordingly. Because at the end of the day, it’s all about addressing the key pain points of customers, and using your technology to deliver to the business outcome you’re looking for.
In general, how are CMOs doing with AI implementation?
I think CMOs are a little bit ahead of finance or supply chain. I see more CMOs experimenting with AI technology, whether it’s content creation or creating images, brand creatives or videos. But I think across all the business functions, we’re still in early days. The business functional teams—whether they’re sales, service or marketing—are all experimenting with AI technology. But we’re very early in identifying exactly what business outcomes we should be shooting for, and what are the quantifiable business benefits that you can achieve using AI technology.
What I see from customers is they’re very curious and interested in how AI could change the way they do things for sales or service. I would say across a company, it is true that I don’t see a lot of enterprise-wide deployment of AI technology. Typically, CMOs ask us to work with a particular sub-group, whether it’s the brand team or the campaign execution team, to test all the technology. Right now, there’s a lot of experimentation. The market sentiment I see is a lot of curiosity, a huge amount of excitement about the potential, and the commitment from the C- level to continuing to experiment with AI so we can eventually show the business outcomes and measurable business impact.
Where is the CMO’s biggest challenge with AI today? Is it getting on board to use it? Is it making team members excited about using it? Is it training? Is it getting everything from a technology standpoint in place to be able to use it? Is it talking people with huge immediate expectations down to reality? Or is it something else entirely?
I think it’s a little bit all of the above, depending on where you are in the organization. AI is still relatively new, so at the end user level, there are a lot of team members in marketing that are experimenting with ChatGPT or any AI tools to create content. They’re using AI to create images, and they’re using AI, for example, to write their entire campaign, fine tune your campaign strategy, but that’s more at the end user level. At the CMO level, the marketing leadership level, I don’t think we’re at the point where there is a concerted AI strategy. What I see companies do is they start with pockets of the marketing team. They start experimenting, they gather the end user input, and they use that to fine tune their AI outlook and strategy. I don’t think we’re at the point where we can say, ‘OK, these are all the areas that AI can add value, and these are things other customers have done.’ It’s very similar to adopting any new technology. There’s a lot of experimentation, a lot of conversations across the CMO community and marketing teams, but also a lot of excitement and curiosity.
How much more time or what kind of examples do you think need to be out there in order to move to that next level where there can be more strategy, and teams can do more than making plans?
I think it comes down to really working with the customers to identify the tangible business outcomes that we can use to market the other customers who are on the same journey, and also documenting some of the best practices, whether it’s about buying criteria, or how do you make decisions about AI technology. What should you be looking for, and the change management process? For the CMOs, just like all the other buyers that are considering AI solutions, collectively, we’re all looking for more guidance on how we select AI technology, what business outcomes should we be shooting for, and how do we manage change with the end user as well as the organization?
Drawing from your experience, what do you think some of the best uses of AI in marketing are?
Within the team I was leading at Microsoft, the areas we’d been using AI is, number one, content creation: Aggregating data from different sources and using that data combined with a large language model to create, whether it’s campaign content or messaging and positioning. The second one is around creative assets, whether it’s videos or imagery. I see teams experimenting with that. The third one, and this is where Gong can play a key role, is to gain a better understanding of the customer. Based on the data entered manually by the sellers or customer service agents, and using that data, you can gain a much more accurate understanding of the customer pain points and the kind of solution they're looking for, and craft your messaging and positioning accordingly. Then, in the same vein, also use the customer interaction data to test how your messaging is being received, whether it resonates with the customer or not, and fine tune that [in] real time, as well.
What should CMOs know about AI?
When it comes to AI, you go through the same process of using any technology, which is you kind-of start small and you gather input from your end users and from your customers. Once you know this is something that’s working or resonating, then you deploy that across the company so you can scale your solution. I think, in that regard, it is similar to how other technology has been adopted.
With AI, it is a new way of working. In the past, a lot of the marketing tech, marketing execution engines relied on marketeers or sellers entering the data into the system, and then retrieve the data manually. Whether it’s email campaigns or any other campaign, there’s a lot of manual data. With AI, it’s a completely different world. So you really need to reimagine how you do marketing. Instead of manually capturing data, you want to focus on aggregating all the data sources that will keep you an accurate picture of customers. You probably want to rethink your data strategy, how you can aggregate your customer data in one platform, then using that data to gain customer insights and to guide marketers and sellers on the next best action they can use to engage with customers.

title: AI Compute Bottleneck: Case For Decentralization If Ever There Was One
text:
The rapid development of AI over recent years, and particularly the rate at which Open AI seems to keep churning out new iterations of its GPT model, make it easy to assume that the technology will continue on a fairly linear trajectory as it matures – perhaps similar to the evolution of the internet. However, there are currently forces at play that could seriously disrupt such a path, hampering the development of the technology or limiting access to it.
Perhaps the biggest and most imminent risk is that demand for computing power to feed AI algorithms could outstrip available supply – and soon. Our World in Data shows that across virtually all domains, compute requirements to feed AI algorithms are increasing exponentially. Meanwhile, there are questions over whether the supply of GPUs will be sufficient – even accounting for factors such as Moore’s Law resulting in increased capacity.
Another challenge is capability. For instance, parallel processing using multiple GPUs is one way to alleviate the problem, but there are limitations on the extent to which this can be done within a single system at scale, due to diminishing benefits and increasing costs.
However, a more pressing problem is the availability of hardware. Demand for microchips started to outweigh supply during the pandemic, even before ChatGPT burst onto the market in 2022. However, geopolitical tensions have since ratcheted up, creating the potential for significant disruption to AI supply chains.
A key consideration is that Taiwan is currently the base for over two-thirds of the global semiconductor industry, and an even larger majority for the most advanced microchips. US-imposed controls over Chinese imports have recently led one Taiwanese operator to exit the mainland Chinese semiconductor market, citing geopolitical uncertainties. Some even speculate that Taiwan’s dominance over the semiconductor industry is the more pragmatic, yet less-discussed root of the US-China dispute, which is more frequently linked to disagreements over the island’s sovereignty.
Regardless of the geopolitical arguments, this is a case for decentralization if ever there was one. Few could argue that AI development – or the means thereto – should be controlled by any one jurisdiction or become the direct subject of a geopolitical wrangling. Furthermore, the decentralization of AI compute can help to overcome some of the challenges involved in scaling centralized data centers, as io.net, a Solana-based project, does.
The project aggregates GPUs from places they may be underutilized, such as data centers, crypto miners, and other DePIN networks such as Filecoin
HyperCycle is another decentralized project looking to tackle the shortfalls of existing compute solutions. It uses cryptographic proofs to enable scalable AI-to-AI communication on a peer-to-peer basis, thus increasing the efficiency of learning algorithms with faster access to compute. The project has signed up nearly 350,000 nodes to its network, each of which can support 150 AI agents that can then communicate and interact with the rest of the network with a 300 millisecond transaction finality.
Feeding demand for AI compute is necessary for companies and nations to stay ahead of the AI game, but history shows us that the opportunities of technological developments are greater when they’re shared. Decentralization is one way to ensure that AI development isn’t controlled or dominated by any entity or jurisdiction while overcoming the existing challenges of centralized systems that are failing to keep pace with growing needs.

title: Qiskit 1.0: A Milestone For The World’s Most Popular Quantum Software
text:
IBM has introduced the 1.0 release of Qiskit, a software stack for quantum computing that includes a hardware-agnostic, open-source software development kit. More importantly, it simplifies quantum programming. Qiskit 1.0 enables users to build and compile circuits with 100-plus qubits, and—as indicated by IBM’s long-term quantum roadmap—it lays the groundwork for future 1,000-plus-qubit workloads. Other notable changes in this release improve its stability policy, release cycles and versioning.
The Qiskit stack aims to help users discover new quantum algorithms, explore computational spaces where quantum excels and support the integration of quantum and classical resources in a quantum-centric supercomputing paradigm.
The interface for Qiskit 1.0 has also been revised based on user feedback to better adapt it to how it is used in practice. One of Qiskit’s significant changes is its formal adoption of semantic versioning. This is important because, throughout the lifecycle of the 1.x release series, the project will be committed to maintaining backward compatibility for publicly documented APIs.
Qiskit’s Development And Reach
Over its seven-year history, Qiskit has made significant contributions to quantum computing. Since its first release in 2017, IBM has tested, iterated and improved more than a hundred Qiskit point-releases. Today, Qiskit has evolved from a quantum SDK into a comprehensive software stack aimed at maximizing performance on advanced quantum hardware and enabling the discovery of quantum algorithms and applications.
Qiskit has a large and growing community of users. It has been downloaded more than 6 million times, and more than 550,000 users have also used Qiskit to construct and execute over 3 trillion quantum circuits. With those stats, it is easy to understand why many users view Qiskit as the de facto standard for creating, optimizing and executing quantum circuits and operators.
Qiskit 1.0 Capabilities
When Qiskit 1.0 came out, it became compatible with the new release of Qiskit Runtime, a quantum app that uses containers to increase computing efficiency by eliminating back-and-forth trips between separated quantum resources and classical resources. Among other things, this speeds up the number of quantum circuits that can be run in a given time.
Components of the Qiskit stack include the Qiskit SDK 1.x, AI-powered circuit optimization via the Qiskit Transpiler Service, execution modes via the Qiskit Runtime Service, a Qiskit Code Assistant and a serverless tool called Qiskit Serverless.
As another plus, Qiskit 1.0 provides users access to IBM’s fleet of quantum systems, including a 133-qubit Heron processor and multiple 127-qubit Eagle processors. If a user has a preference for a different system or is interested in comparing different quantum computers, Qiskit can run on hardware from Alpine Quantum Technologies, Amazon Braket, IonQ, IQM, Quantinuum and Rigetti.
Over seven years, IBM has learned what’s helpful in Qiskit and what isn’t. In some ways, Qiskit has become smaller even though the company has added more features. IBM has started trimming down excess applications and focusing on a smaller set of features representing users' fundamental needs.
Changes To Qiskit 1.0 Primitives
IBM developed Sampler and Estimator primitives in earlier versions of Qiskit Runtime to optimize how code is sent to a quantum computer. The Sampler primitive samples from the output of a quantum circuit, returning bitstrings. Meanwhile, as its name implies, Estimator includes expected values of quantum operators so that users can calculate and interpret these values, which are needed for many algorithms.
The Estimator’s interface has been updated to make it convenient for users who want to use one circuit and many observables, which is the predominant use case. It has different execution modes that allow a user to tailor its interaction with hardware to match application needs.
In Qiskit 1.0, these primitives have been reversioned as SamplerV2 and EstimatorV2. Besides other advantages, these components make it easier to run complex quantum experiments by allowing more data to be handled simultaneously. Here are some of the updates:
- Vectorized inputs make it easier for users to perform experiments with different parameters and observables. Vectors also allow users to run many different experiments at once and simultaneously collect all the results, making the whole process much more efficient.
- Primitive Unified Blocs is a new concept introduced in Qiskit 1.0. A PUB is a group that contains circuits, parameters (values that can change in each experiment) and observables (what you’re measuring). The new system allows multiple PUBs to be inputted at once. Each PUB will be processed separately but within a single job.
- EstimatorV2 has a “precision” argument that lets users specify measurement accuracy. SamplerV2 has a “shots” argument determining how often each experiment will be repeated. Specifying the precision of measurements provides more detailed results from experiments.
Other significant changes in Qiskit 1.0 relate to policy stability, release cycles and versioning. Qiskit 1.0 will have less-frequent breaking changes and better bug support, and it will provide better backward compatibility to support earlier releases.
In earlier iterations of Qiskit, when quantum research was ramping up, it was essential to have tools that could rapidly adapt. Quantum is still a nascent field, so we do still need tools with rapid adaptability—but it doesn’t have to be so fast. Rather, we need it to be more stable and reliable for users trying to use these tools for research and operational work.
The Xs, Ys And Zs Of Semantic Versioning
One of the reasons that IBM has committed to an 18-month support cycle for each major version of Qiskit is that it has officially changed to semantic versioning, which has three components designated as X.Y.Z.
X represents a major version that can be issued once a year. It is the only release that can contain breaking changes to the Qiskit SDK.
Minor versions (Y) will come between major version releases and will be released about every three months. Bug support for previous minor releases will end once a new minor version is published.
As needed, IBM will release patch versions (Z) to publish backward-compatible bug fixes. These releases will come out as needed as bugs are identified. No new deprecations, features or public API changes will be made between these patch versions.
IBM also plans to further improve Qiskit security and usability. That plan includes a six-month support overlap when a new major version is released to provide a transition period between major versions. The release schedule was designed with those plans in mind.
Improving Implementation Of Quantum Algorithms And Applications
IBM is also working on a plan to increase Qiskit’s ability to help users implement quantum algorithms and applications. Qiskit already has a robust framework for understanding the complexity of quantum algorithms. The process includes mapping, optimizing, executing and post-processing. To improve the overall process, IBM is examining and tweaking each step.
Qiskit provides a robust circuit and operator toolkit in the mapping step. Qiskit 1.0 allows users to create a wider variety of circuits, including dynamic circuits that can change during operation. It also supports the creation of larger circuits because it has reduced the memory footprint of Qiskit’s quantum circuit by 32x. IBM plans to reduce that footprint even further, but this is a significant step towards enabling users to work with larger, utility-scale circuits within its system constraints.
IBM provides examples of dynamic circuits that can be created with OpenQASM and its more expressive circuit construction features. Elements such as branches, loops and classical expressions now have native support within the Python-based circuit SDK.
The company has also improved the ability to import and export OpenQASM circuits, which facilitates the exchange of other tools as well. Suppose a user must use a different tool to construct or transpile circuits. In that case, the OpenQASM import/export feature links Qiskit and the broader quantum software ecosystem.
IBM has also made significant progress in memory reduction, as demonstrated by the system measurements while running variational algorithms with TwoLocal circuits, a classic ansatz for certain variational algorithms. This reduction in memory usage is a major improvement because it allows more complex or larger quantum circuits to run, potentially leading to more powerful quantum computations. The reduction is achieved mainly by reusing data and converting some essential parts of Qiskit's quantum circuit structure into Rust rather than Python. Basically, it’s a Python interface to Rust internals.
So, can this technique of reducing memory usage in Qiskit potentially be used to achieve quantum advantage? After all, it allows more complex or larger quantum circuits to be run and results in more powerful quantum computations.
The problem is that achieving quantum advantage also depends on many other factors, including the specific problem being solved, the design of the quantum algorithm and the capabilities of the quantum hardware. So while this technique might be a step forward, it's only one part of a more extensive set of strategies and technologies needed to achieve quantum advantage.
Optimization With Rust
Qiskit’s transpiler and pass manager infrastructure now allow users to compose an optimization pipeline by connecting different components. In support of this, it has taken IBM two years to make the performance improvements needed to convert Qiskit from a pure Python project to one with Rust inside. This process involved identifying hotspots and converting performance bottlenecks into Rust.
The new Qiskit stack has enabled several performance improvements, such as 16x faster circuit optimization, 3x memory usage reduction, 5x faster utility-scale workloads and 40% reduction in circuit depth using AI and heuristic passes.
Internally, Qiskit represents circuits as graphs, with each operation in the quantum circuit being a node in a directed graph. Graph manipulations are the core of every algorithm and the core data structure that every algorithm in the transpiler needs to work with. The system conversion process started by replacing a pure Python graph representation library with a new Rust library for representing and manipulating graphs. This process is still ongoing, but efforts have already yielded impressive results.
Most of what is provided in the package that runs locally on a user’s laptop for circuit optimization are heuristic methods. The problem of taking an input quantum circuit and its more abstract form and finding the optimal circuit is an NP-hard classical problem. So, the doable task becomes finding efficient approximate methods and efficient heuristic methods that provide good, but not necessarily optimum, circuits.
Qiskit And AI
The Qiskit Transpiler Service is now available to premium customers. Qiskit is already equipped with robust and best-of-breed approximations. IBM is now supplementing hand-crafted algorithms with AI and machine learning techniques.
The above graph shows the result of Qiskit’s built-in passes versus the new AI approach. There are specific circuits where it effectively produces equivalent outputs. Still, there's a much broader range of circumstances where AI reinforcement learning methods beat human-generated heuristics.
Wrapping Up
The Qiskit stack supports IBM's Quantum Development and Innovation Roadmap for error-corrected systems. The stack enables open, iterative and collaborative development of quantum algorithms and applications across industries and domains. The release of Qiskit 1.0.0 SDK is one of the most significant quantum milestones after seven years of incremental improvements.
Qiskit 1.0 eliminates old technical issues accumulated over seven years of development. If you look at the documentation, you’ll notice that the Qiskit 1.0.0 release is free of deprecation warnings, and that the upgrade section is longer than usual. These details are directly related to the technical debt cleanup.
As IBM continues to scale Qiskit for larger qubit counts and circuit sizes to match the quantum roadmap, maintaining the balance between Qiskit performance and usability will be an ongoing challenge. To this end, IBM has just begun to integrate AI and machine learning techniques into core Qiskit features such as circuit optimization. While this approach shows promise, further integration of AI into Qiskit development is still an emerging area with open questions about scalability and interpretability. However, success in this area will produce major benefits and increased functionality for users in future versions.
