title: Council Post: How AI Can Transform The IT Service Industry In The Next 5 Years
text:
CTO of Softengi with 30 years of experience in software development, business applications implementation and digital strategy creation.
The ascent of artificial intelligence (AI) heralds a seismic shift that will likely reverberate across all sectors. The IT service industry stands at the forefront, primed for significant upheaval in areas like workforce qualification, service portfolio and business processes.
From the people's perspective, AI's rising tide promises to reshape the workforce landscape, augmenting human capabilities to perform work-related activities more effectively. The service portfolios are set to evolve profoundly, with AI-enabled solutions offering unprecedented customization and scalability. Moreover, processes within IT service organizations are slated for optimization and automation, streamlining workflows and enhancing productivity.
People
First and foremost, all IT services rely on the expertise of individuals who deliver solutions. New AI tools can help enhance day-to-day task performance, from creating business analysis documents to writing software code. As a result, productivity will likely improve as AI-enhanced tools empower the workforce to plunge swiftly into specific use cases. As AI tools enable rapid immersion into specific scenarios, I believe professionals possessing broad, general knowledge rather than deep specialization will be in great demand.
In this way, generalists with a wide-ranging skill set and the ability to quickly adapt to new topics may be more sought after than narrowly focused specialists. Profound general knowledge and creative thinking paired with AI tools can help enable employees to achieve greater outcomes as their skills are more transferable among jobs.
As AI also stands to accelerate a shift in education towards denser, faster-paced learning, students can be better positioned to enter the workforce and provide services earlier than anticipated. Further skill acquisition can then occur on the job.
Service Portfolios
In terms of service portfolios, there will likely be a shift towards optimizing the value gained from both new and established solutions by efficiently utilizing AI tools, applications and services for specific purposes. Service providers may place more emphasis on building reusable intellectual property (IP) assets, including knowledge bases, solutions customized for particular needs and frameworks aimed at enhancing performance.
Services aimed at the following will likely be key areas of business focus moving forward:
Adopting Innovations
Many AI services will facilitate companies' digital transformation into AI-powered entities. This includes assessing organizational readiness, developing AI strategies and implementing AI solutions tailored to specific business objectives.
Legacy App Modernization
With the increasing demand for intelligent, data-driven applications, a vast market of services is emerging to streamline the modernization of legacy applications using AI-powered technologies.
Education And Training
More organizations are beginning to prioritize change management to ensure smooth transitions amidst AI adoption. This includes comprehensive training programs, workshops and consultancy aimed at upskilling employees, building a culture of continuous learning and nurturing talent capable of leveraging AI technologies.
Cybersecurity
Rapid AI adoption can help pave the way for services addressing emerging threats and challenges associated with AI. There will be a growing need for AI solutions for threat detection, prevention and response.
Responsible AI
Compliance services will emphasize ethical AI practices and regulatory compliance to ensure transparency, fairness and accountability in AI-driven decision-making processes.
Processes
As AI technologies automate routine tasks and consolidate workflows, productivity levels are expected to soar within the next few years, potentially reducing the historical advantage of offshoring locations. For example, software coding and QA roles that once required extensive manual labor may be automated, reducing the dependence on offshore contractors for labor-intensive activities.
The shift towards automation stands to optimize service delivery processes, though it may also necessitate a reevaluation of workforce skill sets and talent management strategies. As companies adapt to the AI-driven approach, strategic resource allocation will become paramount, enabling organizations to reallocate personnel to higher-value activities and drive sustainable growth.
With AI becoming more dependent on accessing a company's data, many services will begin to rely on it more regularly. To access and analyze data proficiently, I believe engineers and consultants will begin to spend more time working onsite with the customer data inside the designated premises.
Predictions For The Future Of IT Service Industry Transformation
The IT industry is expected to undergo a significant transformation. Starting with a period of disruption in 2024, the industry is expected to see a major reallocation in 2025, where Global 2000 (G2000) organizations will allocate over 40% of core IT spending towards AI initiatives. However, despite these substantial investments, large enterprises still may struggle to fully leverage their AI capabilities due to inadequate emphasis on employee skill training.
Many large corporations will emerge as key players in the IT service market, driven by their investments in innovative technologies and AI-driven services. This evolution may position these firms at the forefront of the industry, significantly altering the competitive landscape and setting new standards for technological integration and customer service excellence.
Conclusion
Over the next five years, I believe AI will be at the heart of business operations, promoting even greater industry efficiency, agility and innovation. While presenting growth opportunities, this transformation may require companies to reassess their market strategies. It's a big change, but it's full of opportunities for further IT service industry development.

title: Council Post: How Synthetic Data Advances And Protects LLM Development
text:
Fabiana Clemente is the cofounder and CDO of YData. Generative AI and Privacy are their fields of work.
The evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has seen a massive expansion across various sectors, including healthcare, finance, software development and more. However, the success of models such as large language models (LLMs) hinges critically on access to large, diverse and high-quality datasets, which are often limited due to privacy concerns, data scarcity and the high costs of data collection and annotation.
To mitigate these challenges, synthetic data has emerged as an effective solution. And nowadays more than ever, we hear about synthetic data pretty much everywhere. From Google's recently released scientific articles, all the way to Mark Zuckerberg's recent interview, synthetic data seems to be the next big thing that will help harness the full power of LLMs. But what is synthetic data? What are the pros and cons, and how can organizations leverage it?
What You Need To Know
Synthetic data is artificially generated data that replicates the characteristics and patterns of real-world data, allowing for the development of robust, reliable and fair AI models. This data can be generated through algorithms, generative models or simulations, providing a scalable, cost-effective alternative to traditional data collection methods.
Key Benefits And Applications Of Synthetic Data
Synthetic data can be a cost-effective alternative to the collection of real data. There are several benefits and applications for synthetic data when it comes to the development of LLM apps:
• Reasoning: Synthetic data is currently boosting both math and code generation applications. Recent developments in mathematical reasoning for LLMs have shown that the complexity and format of synthetic questions and answers significantly impact model performance.
Projects like Xwin-Math's expansion of synthetic data and MMIQC's integration of this data with high-quality mathematical pre-training data have proven effective in improving model capabilities, demonstrating the benefits of strategic data augmentation in mathematical AI applications.
When it comes to code, the story is not different; the integration of curated synthetic data generation has already proven to boost the performance of models such as CodeRL and CodeAlpaca.
• Tool-Using And Planning: If you want to apply generative AI in the context of tooling use, synthetic data can be used to overcome the limitation of gathering real-world data from users, which is not only time-consuming but can also be biased. Projects like Toolformer and Galactica use synthetic trajectories to train LLMs for API usage, showing incredible improvements regarding tool selection and use.
• Multimodality: There are several use cases for multimodality, from text to image to image to text—you name it. For this type of application, the accuracy of the pairs used for the training is crucial for the success of the applications. For that reason, we see GPT-4 and other models being currently trained with curated synthetic data, proving a performance enhancement in what concerns generalization.
• Multilingualism: From back-translation to multilingual question-and-answer activities, the generation of synthetic data supports the demand for diversity and variability within training sets, thereby accelerating the development of more robust models. These models can be used for applications like chatbots and customer service.
• Alignment: When it comes to applications that can help team productivity, like content creation, documentation creation or even the navigation of internal knowledge management systems, the use of synthetic data can serve as a promising approach for training instruction following models, particularly in cases where real data is scarce, lack diversity or it is just too hard to get.
• Privacy: Synthetic data helps mitigate privacy issues by creating anonymized datasets that do not contain sensitive personal information, which is particularly vital in sensitive domains like healthcare.
Synthetic data is not only useful for developing and enhancing the performance of applications, but it can also play a significant role in evaluations. Synthetic data facilitates the creation of controlled scenarios, aiding in the evaluation processes for factors such as factuality, safety and accelerating human-in-the-loop assessments.
Challenges And Mitigation Strategies
But as with any groundbreaking technology, there are challenges and cons that organizations should consider while adopting synthetic data to enhance generative AI initiatives:
• The Nature Of Synthetic Data: Regardless of how good synthetic data is, you want to make sure that users are informed and aware that it is indeed synthetic data.
• Evaluation Systems: Ensure that your synthetic data generation—similar to using the real data—is validated in terms of quality, fidelity and even privacy. After all, you want to ensure that you have not introduced new biases.
• Establishing Expectations: Establishing clear expectations for the use and timing of synthetic data involves defining specific guidelines that outline not only the scenarios in which synthetic data is appropriate but also the optimal times for its deployment. This approach ensures that synthetic data is used strategically to enhance data-driven projects, avoiding potential pitfalls such as data misuse and ensuring that it contributes positively to achieving project goals.
The Synthetic Future
The future of generative AI and LLMs is tied to the strategic use of synthetic data. It not only addresses privacy concerns by replicating realistic scenarios without personal data but also allows for the training of AI on diverse and extensive datasets, enhancing model robustness and fairness. Moreover, it provides a cost-effective alternative for generating large volumes of data, overcoming the barriers posed by data collection and annotation.
While there are challenges, such as ensuring data authenticity and managing ethical and regulatory implications, these are increasingly being addressed through technological advancements and evolving frameworks. The use of synthetic data opens the door to a promising path forward, promoting innovation while ensuring AI development is both powerful and responsible.
The ongoing focus is to refine the application of synthetic data, optimizing its use in scenarios where it can significantly enhance the efficacy and applicability of AI technologies across various sectors.

title: Council Post: Technology: A Partner For Navigating The Future Of Work
text:
Global Managing Director, Digital Trust Consulting at British Standards Institution (BSI).
When I entered the workforce, the prevailing expectation was that careers spanned roughly 40 years. But with the proportion of the world's population over 60 set to almost double by 2050, many of us are likely to be working into our 70s or beyond. And indeed, as life expectancy grows and as medical developments help us remain healthier and active, why wouldn’t we want to stay employed for longer? Why wouldn’t we want to continue to contribute and remain productive?
This demographic shift is happening in tandem with wider transformations prompted by AI. And it’s worth considering what role AI can play in addressing the implications of this increasingly age-diverse workforce.
AI's Growing Workplace Impact
It’s no exaggeration to say AI is already changing the workplace, whether from machine learning tools, process automation or more. Forecasts suggest global AI investment will be near $200 billion by 2025. That might be businesses creating and using technology we can barely conceive of, but it might be as simple as using automatic transcription or ChatGPT. Either way, AI’s impact is already being felt, both in the knowledge economy and vocational sectors. BSI research last year found that 38% of people said their job already used AI—a figure likely rising every day.
In areas like recruitment, customer services and risk management, AI is already shaping the workplace. In others, that impact is set to grow. The key reason is efficiency. AI’s ability to digest and distill data at pace, provide decision support and simulate scenario analysis is seeing traditionally time-consuming tasks be automated or simplified, from invoicing to managing customer data.
An Age-Diverse Era
Just as we are asking questions about what work will look like when AI is embedded, we have the opportunity to ask questions today about what shape the workforce will take when shared by a greater number of age groups.
At BSI, we believe now is a key moment to do so. We surveyed nearly 1,000 business leaders globally to understand what they feel are the key elements to prioritize so individuals can thrive and organizations can grow as greater numbers work beyond 65.
Evolving Together: Flourishing in the age-diverse workforce identifies a consistent desire for flexibility and support to maintain the good health and well-being that is critical to sustaining 50-year careers. Importantly, there was a consistent emphasis on employers empowering people to retrain for new positions, including transitioning out of manual roles, and a desire for work to be kept interesting and challenging.
AI is no silver bullet, but it can play a part in helping to address these points as the workforce diversifies. It can free experienced workers from less enjoyable or desirable activities by taking on manual tasks and reducing physical labor. In BSI’s poll last year, 54% said AI can be used most effectively to take on work humans don't have time for. In other words, technology can complement individuals’ contributions to boost overall productivity.
The built environment is a case in point. With many manual roles (although not all), it is facing specific pressures as retirement outpaces new recruitment, prompting concerns around skills gaps. In Germany, for example, predictions suggest the sector will face a shortfall of 100,000 by 2030. Just over a tenth of Japanese construction workers are under 30, while only about 10% of the U.S. workforce is under 25.
Technology—especially where it can relieve workers of physical roles—will be critical. This could be tools like drones assisting in monitoring safety, predictive trend data or modeling. By partnering with AI, a world of opportunity could be opened to retain experienced workers and find new ways to leverage their skills.
Developing An AI-Skilled Workforce
In the discussion around the future of work, AI could step forward as a game-changer, blending human creativity with cutting-edge technology to shape a new workforce. Human oversight of AI outputs could become the way of the future, whereby employees feel fully comfortable understanding AI’s decision-making logic and overruling or pausing operations when necessary.
For this to happen, a steady supply of skilled workers will be key. And with a shrinking pool of new workers entering the labor market, there will be impetus for businesses and policymakers to ensure they develop those skills. In our study, business leaders emphasized the necessity of upskilling people with new tools as the age-diverse workforce becomes a reality. They ranked access to training and skills development as a top-five priority in terms of individual needs and providing opportunities for retraining people to new roles or supporting returnships as a top-five priority for organizations.
There was also strong support for policymakers offering financial incentives to encourage businesses to invest in retraining and skills development. There is a key opportunity to enable experienced workers to remain productive for longer and flourish in the future workplace with skills maintenance and development, especially as relates to AI.
With both AI and the age-diverse workforce, we are facing an unknown. We don’t yet know how these changes will shape our future. But we can take steps now to ensure they are a force for good. Individuals, organizations and policymakers have the opportunity to embrace AI to respond to the changing workforce.
AI can be a powerful tool to help support meaningful careers and sustainable work throughout everyone’s lifetime—provided we put training in place now to ensure individuals can thrive and remain productive throughout their work span and give organizations the confidence to grow.

title: Council Post: The Rise Of Social Shopping And The Opportunity Ahead
text:
Raj De Datta is CEO of Bloomreach, a platform that personalizes the e-commerce experience, and the author of "The Digital Seeker."
Social media has long shaped consumer shopping habits, but as of late, its role in the buying journey has taken on new meaning for brands and retailers. Social commerce—the fusion of content and commerce—is fast expanding e-commerce possibilities beyond traditional web and app channels.
Projected to hit a $1.2 trillion market value by 2025, social commerce enables businesses to sell products and services directly on a social platform (indirect social commerce also enables businesses to drive buyers to their site through social content). With nearly 5 billion users worldwide, that presents a unique chance to establish direct connections with customers and drive significant revenue.
Social platforms are well aware of how enticing that potential is to businesses. TikTok purportedly aims to grow its U.S. e-commerce volume tenfold to $17.5 billion by 2024. Its launch of TikTok Shop has garnered mixed reactions from businesses, but in a Consumer Trends survey from The New Consumer, 69% of surveyed TikTok users said they were willing to buy something from the platform. Others are taking proactive action to make social selling easier, such as Pinterest, which has introduced an API for shopping that includes additional catalog management and metadata capabilities to improve product information.
With such vast potential and buy-in from the platforms themselves, social commerce seems like an area every e-commerce business should be focused on. But why is now the right time to invest in this strategy—and what might stand in the way of success?
Trust Challenges
The trust challenges of social commerce remain one of the biggest roadblocks for businesses adopting this channel. Despite the increasing amount of time consumers spend on social media and the data they share to make that experience more enjoyable, sentiment changes when a purchase is involved.
Nearly 4 in 10 customers hold back from social media purchases over concerns about how platforms manage personal data. Although they may discover a product on a social platform, consumers will often navigate outside of the social platform to a trusted brand’s website to make a purchase. This added step in the buying journey creates more opportunities for customers to abandon their purchase entirely.
This trust gap may shift with time, though. Even amid concerns today, many platforms are still seeing incremental shopping growth, showing that consumers really do want to embrace this channel.
For older generations of shoppers, trust will likely grow as bigger brands begin to adopt social commerce. An Accenture survey found this generation of shoppers values security and brand familiarity—two areas where big-name brands can deliver. Younger generations, meanwhile, put more faith in buyer reviews. Brands that can provide consistent value—which will include transparent returns and refunds—can garner trust even without a big name as customers share their positive experiences with others.
AI Opportunities
Despite the trust challenges facing social commerce, there really has never been a better time for businesses to take a serious look at their social strategies. While social commerce has been around for some time now, it's the latest innovations in AI that are giving businesses the best opportunity to succeed in this channel.
AI offers sizable advantages in three key areas of social: scale, discoverability and engagement. Here’s how those could come to life on different platforms:
• Instagram: For businesses with smaller marketing teams, developing social strategies and content can be a massive undertaking. Generative AI can take on much of that work, though. On the creative side, it can augment product photos to better capture attention visually. For the post descriptions, generative AI can write content that matches both brand tone and customer voice.
And of course, it can do this for an entire week’s worth of posts in mere minutes. While brands may not be ready to share those posts blindly, it gives a strong foundation of scalable social strategy for time-strapped teams to start with.
• TikTok: With a strong understanding of their customer data, a business can use AI to maximize the discoverability of their content on TikTok. After defining their high-value customer segments, businesses can use AI to generate hashtags and descriptions that are most relevant to the audience they’re trying to reach. Adding these layers to a post can give the algorithm a better understanding of who this content is intended for, increasing your discoverability for key audiences.
• Meta: With 2.9 million monthly active users, Meta offers no shortage of customer engagement opportunities, particularly as customers start conversations via comments. But today, it’s impossible for businesses to actually engage with every customer comment, which can deter shoppers who were looking for additional guidance before making a purchase.
Soon though, generative AI is going to offer some conversational use cases that will enable that level of engagement. This could very well include shopping assistants who can respond to customer comments and offer one-to-one guidance, at scale, within social platforms like Meta.
The Opportunity Ahead
The shopping journey has been evolving for many years to meet customers where they are. From the store to the web, commerce has continued to adapt to new channels and new ways of reaching customers. Social commerce is yet another continuation of this, taking shopping to a channel where consumers spend an increasing percentage of their days.
Much as businesses could not ignore the early days of e-commerce, they cannot ignore this new shift to social channels. Consumers may still be hesitant to spend directly on social platforms, but that trust will quickly evolve. The earlier businesses can explore this channel—and where AI can amplify their efforts—the better positioned they’ll be once customers are ready to shop.

title: Council Post: It's Time To Plan For An AI And Quantum Future
text:
CEO of D-Wave.
It's no secret that AI is being adopted and developed at an astonishing rate. According to Stanford University's 2024 AI Index Report, funding for generative AI experienced a significant increase in 2023, jumping to $25.2 billion, marking an eightfold increase from the previous year.
By now, every company (hopefully) has an AI plan in place, but it's time to start thinking about where quantum computing fits into that plan. Companies that can envision how quantum computing and AI could be used together—and invest in both—will be well-positioned to gain a competitive edge by drawing on the technologies' combined advantages while addressing energy demands.
Quantum and AI create an industrial-strength power duo.
How will these two technologies join forces? AI excels in automating tasks and streamlining processes, aiding businesses in making data-driven decisions by uncovering patterns, trends and insights. Meanwhile, quantum computing shines in solving complex optimization problems such as supply chain management, manufacturing efficiency, employee scheduling and emissions reduction.
The two technologies are complementary. Quantum computing is demonstrating how it could enhance AI by enabling more accurate and more efficient model training and leveraging the predictive capabilities of AI to deliver better-optimized business processes. Soon, quantum computing could supercharge AI for certain use cases in a manner that is sustainable in terms of cost and energy.
There are many compelling reasons why leaders need to start thinking now about a quantum computing strategy alongside enterprise AI. What's more, they can take concrete steps to build their quantum and AI future now.
Quantum computers could help develop more accurate AI models.
As AI continues to evolve, the computational resources required to train and deploy the models are growing exponentially. Quantum computing can mitigate some of the challenges posed by the increasing complexity and size of AI models. Imagine being able to use quantum computing to build more accurate and complete models, helping businesses get more out of AI without being constrained by the limitations of classical computing.
For example, in the field of drug discovery, quantum-powered AI models could identify potential new drug candidates by analyzing molecular structures. It could also accelerate the development of new materials by simulating and analyzing their properties at the molecular level—fueling potential breakthroughs in electronics, renewable energy technologies and more sustainable products.
Using quantum computing to train AI models will consume much less power.
AI has made remarkable strides in recent years. However, the technology is limited by the massive amount of energy required to develop and run its algorithms. Estimates from the International Energy Agency indicate that global electricity consumption from AI, data centers and cryptocurrency could double by 2026.
Annealing quantum computing technology has been shown to be more energy-efficient than classical computing for developing advanced AI models. This means quantum computing could help boost AI advancements in areas such as deep learning, natural language processing and computer vision without consuming enormous amounts of energy.
Complex supply chain logistics and manufacturing scenarios can benefit.
Industries such as logistics and manufacturing deal with complex challenges that involve numerous variables and constraints when considering things like inventory management, warehouse capacity and delivery route planning.
AI can make highly accurate sales predictions by analyzing vast amounts of data, considering factors such as historical sales, market trends and consumer behavior. With sustainability now an added business imperative, quantum plus AI could help manufacturing organizations forecast demand more precisely and align production—minimizing the creation of excess goods and reducing waste through the supply chain.
By using quantum to optimize routing, production and inventory management based on AI-powered forecasting, quantum and AI together could help organizations reduce the need for transportation and storage—reducing costs and carbon emissions.
What steps can leaders take now to bring quantum AI into their enterprise?
1. Incorporate quantum now to maximize AI impact.
Quantum computing is not a distant reality but a present opportunity, and leaders should spearhead initiatives that prioritize the exploration and adoption of today's annealing quantum computing alongside efforts to scale AI. Teams can start identifying areas where quantum AI could make an impact today, especially to build more accurate models and more energy-efficient model training. In addition, leaders should invest in quantum AI now to facilitate rapid development and deployment of applications.
2. Engage teams to identify near-term quantum AI use cases.
We're starting to see near-term use cases emerging that are well-suited for quantum AI, most notably in the areas of supply chain logistics, manufacturing and life sciences. Leaders should engage their internal teams to identify where quantum AI can support their specific business challenges. Engaging cross-functional teams to identify problems that are suitable for quantum AI will help not only expedite quantum AI's enterprise impact but also embed a culture of innovation and adaptability.
As quantum hardware scales up and algorithms become more refined, we'll soon live in an era where quantum-powered AI is the norm, offering scalable and energy-efficient solutions to tackle other complex problems like financial modeling and risk assessment or climate modeling and weather prediction.
As author and quantum computing expert Arthur Herman wrote, "What AI can do, AI/quantum will do better." Quantum computing is on track to take AI to the next level when it comes to both performance and sustainability. It's time for organizations to start thinking about where quantum computing fits into their AI plan before the competition does.

title: Embracing AI Across The Marketing Mix
text:
Google has kicked third-party cookie retirement down the road again, but most marketers are already embracing new technologies to bridge the gap. Chief among them — artificial intelligence (AI). This technology has proved to be a game-changer for marketers, automating tedious and mundane tasks and leaving more time for high-level activities. According to Movable Ink’s 2024 Audience of One report, 95% of marketers concur that automating manual tasks enables a more strategy-focused approach.
Companies must act strategically when adopting AI-powered tools. Marketers can’t build their strategy on a single AI function or application. A diversified strategy creates agility to react to market and technology shifts.
“AI is much broader than what you read in the news. The technology provides advantages in a myriad marketing functions, including data insights, personalization, campaign optimization, SEO, idea generation, and short-form content,” said Movable Ink CEO Vivek Sharma. “Marketers who channel its full power will redefine customer engagement, create memorable experiences, and deliver ROI.”
How marketers can use AI
Nearly all organizations leverage AI in their marketing initiatives, integrating it into most channels. AI’s capabilities alleviate many campaign pain points. Here are a few ways companies are using algorithms to their advantage.
Consumer behavior analytics
According to Movable Ink’s report, 6 in 10 marketers currently use AI for consumer behavior analysis. AI's ability to analyze large amounts of customer data provides an in-depth understanding of behavior patterns. This insight extends beyond populations and segments to individuals. Marketers can build campaigns catered to specific preferences, anticipate future needs, and create a tailored customer experience.
“Understanding consumer behavior builds the foundation for effective marketing,” said Sharma. “The ability to predict and proactively address customer needs will be a key differentiator for successful marketing strategies.”
- Content creation
GenAI is on everyone’s radar right now. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, 77% of people have heard of this technology, and 19% have tried it. Content creation is a popular use case among users.
About a quarter of marketers use GenAI to create content. Using audience data, the algorithm can generate compelling narratives that resonate with the target audience. But AI should not operate in a vacuum.
“Although AI is a game-changer in copywriting, human creativity is indispensable in crafting messages that hit the mark,” said Sharma. “True magic happens when marketers set the direction, define the rules, and polish the AI-generated content.”
- Personalization
According to McKinsey, about 70% of today’s buyers expect personalized interactions. Nearly all (98%) of marketers agree AI will help deliver more tailored customer experiences, and more than half are already using it for this purpose.
Based on customer behavior analytics, businesses can build curated content, offers, and interactions. AI assists in all facets of message development and delivery, allowing personalization at scale. The data informs content creation, allowing marketers to develop a large set of creative assets aligning with brand voice and catering to varying consumer preferences and buying stages. Algorithms can evaluate consumer behavior to dynamically assemble personalized messages and determine the ideal product recommendations, channels, and send time for each person.
For example, a woman might shop for luxury purses late in the evening. She frequently browses through the available options but hasn’t bought one. AI can analyze her past behavior to determine the messaging most likely to drive a conversion and automatically build a personalized message — delivered in the evening — recommending similar purses at a lower price point, offering her a 10% discount, or showcasing the trendiest designs. AI can also predict what other items she might buy from the catalog, allowing it to deliver tailored suggestions for additional purchases.
Opportunities abound to create personalized experiences. Etsy recently launched a new customization feature called Gift Mode, which leverages GenAI and human curation to deliver a tailored gift guide to help shoppers find the perfect present. Domino’s is also experimenting with AI to enhance its ordering process and offer the right thing to the right customer at the right time.
“AI empowers brands to build a deeper, more meaningful relationship with each customer. In the era of the empowered consumer, personalization is no longer optional – it's the key to driving engagement, loyalty, and growth,” said Sharma.
- Campaign management
Monitoring multiple campaigns presents a significant challenge to marketers with many other responsibilities. AI can track and report on all campaigns simultaneously, highlighting actionable insights to optimize effectiveness. AI-powered analytics deliver granular insight beyond the campaign level, such as specific asset performance. Marketers can adjust accordingly and easily evaluate the impact.
Continuous learning capabilities enable AI to execute automated experimentation and optimization to understand changing customer preferences, resulting in more effective personalization, better engagement, and higher revenue and conversation lift. According to Movable Ink’s data, 95% of marketers agree that AI enables a more streamlined campaign management approach, promoting strategy-focused execution and an opportunity to scale.
These analytics also inform ROI reporting, allowing marketing teams to demonstrate their contributions to the bottom line.
- SEO
AI supercharges SEO. Marketers can leverage it for in-depth keyword research, content optimization, topic suggestions, understanding user behavior, and performance monitoring. Movable Ink's survey showed that 34% of marketers use AI for SEO.
Making a marketer’s life easier
AI relieves the intense pressure on marketers. With AI handling the bulk of data analysis and campaign optimization, marketers have more time to think strategically and be creative. Reducing tedious tasks not only helps business performance — it improves employee morale and job satisfaction. Work is much more fun when you can focus on high-value, creative tasks rather than sort through data-filled spreadsheets.
“We’ve heard people say this before, but we at Movable Ink have seen it to be true — AI helps marketers work smarter and create leverage on their time,” said Sharma.
AI is the future of marketing
Many opportunities for AI in marketing remain untapped. Only about half of the marketers surveyed use AI for advertising, social media, and content marketing, while just more than a third use it for email. AI’s versatility makes it a powerful tool in all of these channels.
As Sharma said, “The future of marketing belongs to those who can harness the power of AI to create truly exceptional experiences.”

title: Even with glitches, planning your next trip with AI is making me rethink travel
text:
With vacation planning, most people fall into two camps: those who love planning and those who hate it.
Artificial intelligence tools like GuideGeek, developed by Matador Network and accessible via Meta's Messenger app, offer a glimpse into a future where vacation planning is as simple as sending a text.
Yet, as we lean into this new era, it's clear that these amazingly powerful tools come with their own set of quirks.
AI travel ‘hallucinations’ can derail a trip
Take, for instance, the phenomenon known as "AI hallucinations." These occur when the AI, attempting to fill gaps in its knowledge, invents answers. A classic example unfolded when an AI-powered assistant was asked about travel details for "Crete Freeze" instead of "Crete, Greece". Instead of clarifying the query, the AI crafted a detailed story about a non-existent ice cream parlor in Pittsburgh. While creative, such responses aren’t particularly useful when you're trying to plan an actual trip.

When tiny missed details turn into big trouble
This isn't an isolated incident. Across the travel industry, AI tools have mistakenly concocted false job histories and even non-existent travel destinations. This tendency can lead to significant travel planning errors, such as suggesting routes that don’t exist or accommodations that are the stuff of fiction.
Why does this happen? AI systems, particularly those based on generative models, strive to provide answers for every query. In doing so, they sometimes create plausible but incorrect information. While these errors are often corrected quickly, they highlight an important aspect of using AI in travel planning: verification is key.

Embracing the new AI travel planning experiment
Matador Network has taken steps to mitigate these errors by introducing stringent checks and balances for GuideGeek. They've reduced the occurrence of hallucinations significantly, from a startling 14% down to a more manageable 2%. They achieved this by enhancing the AI’s training and integrating real-time data from reliable sources like Skyscanner and Expedia.
Despite these improvements, the responsibility ultimately falls on the travel planner to double-check all AI-generated plans. When using AI tools like GuideGeek, it’s prudent to verify the details of your itinerary as you would with a travel agent. Check flight schedules, hotel bookings and travel routes against trusted sources.
Verify any travel plans, whether from AI or a human expert
Incorporating AI into travel planning requires a balanced approach. While these tools can efficiently handle vast amounts of data and provide quick responses, their current propensity for errors cannot be overlooked. People should approach AI-generated travel plans with a healthy dose of both excitement and skepticism, reviewing and confirming details to avoid potential pitfalls.

AI trip planning can open doors you never knew to knock on
The process of integrating AI into travel planning is undoubtedly exciting, and it promises a more streamlined and accessible future for travelers.
Matador Network CEO Ross Borden points to the benefits of AI travel planning, saying, "We all know that typical experience of booking travel online – you've got 30 browser tabs open and a headache. title: Adobe Global Chief Privacy And Cybersecurity Legal Officer Nubiaa Shabaka On Trust, Data Security And AI
text:
While cybersecurity and privacy are two different aspects in dealing with data, Nubiaa Shabaka says they fit well together. She’s a vice president at Adobe, serving as the company’s global chief privacy and cybersecurity legal officer. I talked with her about these two aspects of technology, changes AI is bringing to the way business is done, and what the future holds.
This conversation has been edited for length, continuity and clarity. An excerpt was in Thursday’s Forbes CIO newsletter.
Tell me about your role at Adobe.
Shabaka: I am the chief privacy officer. And so what that means is I lead privacy legal, as well as privacy. Privacy legal does things like give advice, monitor and track the law, help draft contracts, all kinds of legal things. I also lead privacy compliance. Privacy compliance is helping with compliance and training, and policies and standards. I also lead a component of privacy engineering and operations to make sure we have a coordinated effort amongst the many, many engineers in the various groups. If it’s a privacy-specific tool, or something that we need to do from a structural engineering perspective, we have experts that can then work to make sure we’re all coordinated, and we don’t have each group doing their own thing, wasting resources. I then also lead cyber legal, and from a cyber legal perspective, we work with the main coverage attorney for our chief security officer that handles all things security. We advise on all of those cyber laws and policies, and their training, and incidents, and contract language on cybersecurity—whether it’s with our vendors or our customers. So it runs the gamut.
And in all of these areas, we help our government relations team [on] various public policy initiatives in cybersecurity and privacy. Anything that touches upon cybersecurity or privacy, whether it’s the internal team infrastructure, our CIO office, IT or security, or even any of the business units: our digital media or DX business, if it’s privacy and security, we are happy to be involved.
How do you see privacy and security fitting together? Why are they a good pair to have under one person?
I actually was so excited when I was interviewing with our chief trust officer a couple of years ago to understand their structure, because I’ve always had a really attached-at-the-hip relationship with the chief security officer. I’ve been a chief cyber legal officer and the head of privacy or chief privacy officer for many years. It’s so important that it be so connected because you’re able to look over the horizon. You’re able to plan and have the most streamlined and efficient manner to protect Adobe, and give the best trustworthy products to our customers. As well, being so integrated, [you have] weekly meetings, daily chats, invited to each other’s team related off-sites and things of that nature.
It’s really all in the construct of what is trust. You need security, you need privacy. And it all is just so interconnected. If you think about personal information, of course that’s privacy. And security is the assets, the infrastructure and potentially proprietary and IP, but you cannot have privacy without security. Privacy is a huge part, of course, of security. They’re very, very interconnected, and folks who pull it together, who have that close relationship, I think have a better value, not only internally, but also to their customers because of the trust that we’re able to build.
How does AI impact privacy and security?
My whole title is chief cyber and legal officer. I think about my role as those two things and two other things. I also co-lead data governance with our chief information officer and our chief security officer, bringing in all of the applicable business units and risk folks to run data governance. I also am a core member of our AI governance. Privacy and security is just key [for] AI at Adobe, a cross-functional team that has folks from our IT department, our security department, my team, other folks in legal and in strategy, coming together to have this cross-functional AI governance.
How privacy and security is impacted by AI, ooh ooh ooh, the stories you can tell. The concept of good folks and even bad actors are able to just be so much more sophisticated on a proactive and reactive standpoint. AI is here. We really need to incorporate it in a privacy and security conscious fashion, but it will allow us to be more privacy-centric when done correctly, and allow us to be more security-focused, when done correctly, to counterbalance the bad actors. Having security and privacy sit at the table in AI governance really keeps security and privacy top of mind when we roll out AI to make sure they have those appropriate data protection aspects. And any privacy-related tools that we roll out always have the personal privacy considerations in mind to make sure we have the appropriate balancing act and impact assessment.
When done correctly, how can AI make these tools more privacy-centric?
Using AI and various privacy-enhancing technologies, you could have various components built where you do not have to always have a human who might look at these various components and data, then use it for means beyond the intentional or initial designed rationale. You can build code that allows us to have very objective reviews, so long as you’re constantly checking and making sure you [do] not have a bias.
It can go through a lot more data, but if you use synthetic data, if you follow the principles of data minimization in terms of hashing and various other technologies that can learn from the AI without actually having the sensitive data needed, you can get the same elements of improving privacy and security without going into all the specific elements they’re under.
As you’re working to improve privacy. Do you see issues related to AI on the horizon? And not just at Adobe, but in general that could put privacy at risk?
I do think that if privacy and security is not done right, you certainly have an increased amount of data that could run into pitfalls. Talking about what Adobe does to ensure that we do it correctly, ART is our acronym: accountability, responsibility and transparency. Having that cross-functional team and having privacy impact assessments and ethics impacts assessments when it comes to AI, we do in fact have the appropriate governance that puts customers first off in terms of how we incorporate AI into our products.
I agree if you don’t have the skill set, or the trust mindset, and you just want to rush to market and don’t have those principles in place, I think certainly companies could fall into trouble.
With data governance in general, what are some of the bigger issues in privacy you’re seeing right now?
As the world evolves, the convergence of all of these unique disciplines are all coming together. When I have discussions with many of my chief privacy officer colleagues at other companies, it’s interesting how chief privacy officers are often handling the AI because they’re seeing no one else at their company to do that. We have specific folks within Adobe that do AI ethics, and then we cross-functionally manage it.
If you think about what’s going on in the EU, they’re actually proposing and passing laws that treat all data the same as personal information, where you need to have the transparency and you need to have the impact assessments. Or you have security-related incidents and laws proposed and passed that is not just if you have a security incident as it relates to personal information, but if you have any security incident, you need to provide the appropriate transparency. In data governance, what I am seeing is the convergence of what used to be unique disciplines of privacy and security, AI and data governance, whereby it’s all one and it’s all together. They’re very similar principles. It is really fortuitous to be at Adobe, where we have already brought those things together, where I think other companies will be going.
What about security? What are some of the bigger issues there, and how has security changed?
Security’s bad actors get more sophisticated every year, not because they themselves got some advanced degree, but [because of] the networks and security as a service, the concept that even bad actors can outsource toolkits and hacking. It used to be cybercriminals had a certain level of threat, and nation states had a certain level of threat, but when you have this new era of cybercriminals learning from nation states, or nation states on their side, you will see the advancement and sophistication in some of these areas.
You then combine that with AI, and [consider] just the mass amount of attacks that could happen in very short timeframes. That is why if bad actors are using AI and cybersecurity, certainly the good actors need to respond in a reactive manner, and think ahead in a proactive manner to defend. What I’m seeing in security is just a continual advancement of all of these attacks and sophistications. When you think about AI, and you think recent examples of companies paying $25 million via their CFO, which was a deepfake, is very concerning and should be concerning to all companies: If you can be fooled not only by voice, but by image where someone in your company high up is authorizing you to do something.
What is Adobe doing to fight back against people using your tools for this kind of action?
Adobe is a leader in many of these respects. When it comes to deepfakes, for example, our Content Authenticity Initiative with Content Credentials. We have many companies in the tech industry and otherwise, whereby folks can use our tooling in order to indicate the [content’s] credentials, whether it’s original, how it’s been modified, how it was created.
You work in areas in which there are a lot of policymakers paying attention and talking about regulations, but there aren’t really a lot of regulations there. Where do you see things going in terms of AI and privacy regulations in the next year? What is Adobe doing to help these questions get worked out? What are your priorities in these areas?
I would say that there are plenty of regulations that are hard and fast on a sectoral basis. The U.S. has a different mindset than Europe. Europe has [General Data Protection Regulation] and large omnibus rules. The U.S. certainly has sectoral rules that have been around for a very long time. If you think back to 1999, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. I come from a financial services background, and so there are hard-and-fast rules that exist. Now we have omnibus state laws that have somewhat mimicked GDPR, and are different in many ways. We are up to 15 U.S. omnibus state laws, which are hard and fast rules.
The U.S. has been a leader on the security side starting with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, which is optional. Now they are proposing to implement certain items in the U.S. to make hard-and-fast rules. But we certainly have cyber and personal information breach laws in every jurisdiction in the U.S., which is a mitigating factor, right. You don’t want to have to report breaches, so you have appropriate safeguards in order to counterbalance your reporting. We have the new SEC cyber-disclosure laws that came into effect in December of 2023, which is a hard-and-fast rule for disclosure. It is, in fact, a mechanism to have and support appropriate cybersecurity controls.
I do think, even with the rules that we have in place, multinational companies forget about what the rules are just in the U.S. Adobe is a multinational company, and we have to abide by the plethora of rules throughout the Americas and Asia and AMEA. We don’t believe in playing whack-a-mole, following rule by rule and law by law. We look over the horizon to have an appropriate privacy program and cyber program that we stand behind.
On the security side, we have our proprietary Common Controls framework that maps to the various laws around the world from a technical perspective on the privacy and security angle. Adobe’s vision is to set our high water mark, which typically will address any rule, any law that comes into play. That’s how we abide by having the appropriate privacy and security controls.
What I see coming is the additional continual global standard. We are excited about the potential proposed federal privacy law here in the U.S., and encourage governments around the world to continue to work together to promote cross-border data transfers and innovation and technology, while of course balancing privacy and security. Adobe is happy to be part of those conversations through trades and directly meeting with regulators around the world to help move in that direction, whereby we can have innovation and prosperity all together.
Where do you see AI technology going in the next year?
I’m excited about all of the announcements that Adobe has made in the AI space alone, not only with our proprietary Firefly, but also partnering with many of the other AI tools out there to provide our customers with the ability to use Adobe and our integrated platforms to have a one-stop shop. The vision of the integration with other AIs, and how that can enhance Adobe’s systems as well. That’s what I see: more AIs coming together and being more interconnected.

title: An American Industrial Policy For AI Takes Shape
text:
A comprehensive industrial policy has materialized for advanced semiconductors between the CHIPS
An increase in government funding for domestic non-defense AI innovation would drive the promote half of the industrial policy. In the roadmap released earlier this week, the Senate’s bipartisan working group called for appropriations to reach “at least $32 billion per year for (non-defense) AI innovation” as soon as possible. This number was recommended by the National Security Commission on AI in its final report published in 2021. While far greater than the funds appropriated in the CHIPS and Science Act, the resemblance is unmistakable, and it is perhaps then no surprise that two of the Senate’s leading architects behind the two efforts are the same: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.).
The working group’s proposal has yet to be turned into a bill, and it may be a few months before legislative text is published as the senators collect feedback on their roadmap. Still, even when a draft is released, there is no promise that the proposal will pass quickly or at all, especially in the current divided Congress. There is a bipartisan consensus in wanting to support domestic AI innovation, but the high price tag may scare away some more budget-conscious conservatives seeking to lower government spending.
In addition, relatively few, if any, meaningful bills are expected to pass between now and the end of the year, other than must-pass legislation, which leaves only a handful of opportunities for the bill to catch a ride if it is to pass this year. This timing may be okay with the Senate working group as they seem more interested in building a genuine bipartisan consensus than rushing through a partisan version of the legislation. The House also has its own bipartisan AI task force, which is expected to produce its own report on addressing the new technology, giving a better sense of the overlap and divide between the two chambers.
The second part of this industrial policy is to protect the US’s advanced AI models from foreign adversaries, particularly China. According to Reuters, the Commerce Department is considering export controls for the most advanced AI models, similar to what it has done with semiconductors. The rules would limit access to the backend software powering the models but not downstream applications created with the software. The logistics of enforcing these controls is likely to be more difficult than restricting semiconductor sales as no physical product is involved, but this may not stop the Biden administration from moving forward with proposed regulations.
The metrics used to determine which models would fall under these restrictions have yet to be determined. One potential standard from President Joe Biden’s 2023 AI executive order would be the computing power needed to train the model. However, if the measure in the EO were used, no existing models would be covered. Another approach could be to use a lower computer power threshold and consider other factors like the type of data used and the model’s intended use.
While the increased government funding and export control efforts are in their beginning stages, the focus on AI among officials could mean that this industrial policy will come to bear over the next couple of years. The CHIPS and Science Act took a few years to be conceived before it was passed, so it is more than possible for AI to experience a similarly prolonged timeline. The discussions happening now are still crucial to follow as they will shape the contours for future action and indicate lawmakers’ regulatory priorities for the technology and any partisan fault lines that could hamper legislative efforts.

title: 3 High-Income Skills In 2024 That AI Can’t Replace
text:
An estimated 22% of workers stated that they feared the risk of AI (artificial intelligence) taking their job, while 72% of Fortune 500 Chief Human Resources Officers predicted that AI could indeed replace roles within their organization within the next three years, in a recent Gallup survey released in February,
Meanwhile,
According to the survey and Gallup analysis, these fears are underpinned by the FOMO (fear of missing out)—being left behind due to not having the skills to render one capable to meet the demands of AI-driven jobs, in addition to the worry that this new technology will completely eliminate their current roles.
While this fear is certainly valid, you are not completely powerless.
There are things that you can do to reduce the likelihood that you will be caught out, which will strengthen and future-proof your career. For example, approximately 45% of U.S. respondents to an Indeed survey for the Global Future of Work Report upskilled to stay competitive in a tech-driven labor market.
Additionally, 40% of employees have seen employees with entirely different careers enter the market later into their career, the report noted.
For example, you can take time now to develop high-income skills, which require higher levels of specialism and expertise. You should also figure out which skills are irreplaceable by AI, because these will help you to become exceptional in your career, move up the ladder, and/or make a career pivot, regardless of your current job. They can help set you apart from other job candidates, and place you in a favorable position to receive a pay increase, promotion, or gain more business opportunities as a freelancer.
These high-income skills can be applied in a wide variety of contexts, so even if your job becomes obsolete, you can transfer them elsewhere—as long as you start demonstrating them now.
1. Problem-Solving Skills
Problem-solving is something that AI cannot replicate fully. Although there are many ways and tools in which AI can be used to fix problems and perform analysis, problem-solving skills still remain the unique prerogative of human beings, and this skill set is even listed in LinkedIn's Most In-Demand Skills of 2024 report.
This is because although AI can "think" logically and pull up data, it does not excel in creativity and out-of-the-box approaches. This is where you, the human, would come in.
2. Personal Branding Skills
Another hot skill on the rise is personal branding. Personal branding is when you are essentially your own PR agent. You consciously and intentionally influence others' perception of you within your industry, based on the way you project yourself in your job, in your business if self-employed, on social media, and at networking events.
Learning personal branding skills is a powerful tool that can distinguish you from others in your sector, even those who may have more experience than you. Being able to sell yourself confidently and establishing a solid personal brand increases others' trust in you—from stakeholders, to customers, to your employer. Consequently, personal branding skills opens up many new business and career opportunities which would otherwise remain closed.
3. Communication Skills
Communication skills ranks highly as LinkedIn's no.1 skill for 2024, and for good reason. With the increase of remote and hybrid working, and the use of artificial intelligence tools, in addition to multigenerational working, there are plenty of barriers to transparent and collaborative communication.
If you take time to polish your communication skills, learning how to practice active listening, communicate with empathy, and know how to use the right communication tools to get your message across while communicating concisely and with clarity, you will be able to set yourself apart as a highly effective team member, and will be extremely successful in your role as a leader or manager.
With communication, you can negotiate your way to higher pay, motivate team morale and increase performance levels, quell misunderstandings, and present your ideas to gain buy-in from stakeholders. Now that is a skill worth honing. It's pretty easy to see how this correlates with a higher salary or increased earnings.
AI tools can certainly help you refine your communication (as is the case with AI-powered email tools such as Lyne AI), but you need to be careful that you do not depend on it so much that you are unable to communicate effectively in everyday life, offline.
So, should you be worried that AI will take your job? Perhaps. Should you worry that it will take away your career and your chances of securing higher pay? Certainly not.

title: Baidu 'confident' AI will sustain growth after sluggish first quarter - ET Telecom
text:

Baidu 'confident' AI will sustain growth after sluggish first quarter
"While we operate our legacy business in a challenging environment and (expect) slower revenue growth in the near term, we remain confident that AI will help us sustain growth in revenue and profit in the long run," said co-founder and CEO Robin Li in a call to analysts.
By Liam Mo and Yuvraj Malik
China's Baidu said on Thursday it was confident artificial intelligence would help drive future sales and profits after reporting first-quarter revenue growth of just 1% as weak Chinese economic growth kept advertisers cautious.
The company has touted the current fourth version of its GPT-like large language model Ernie - which has undergone several iterations since it was unveiled in March last year - as rivaling OpenAI's GPT-4.
"While we operate our legacy business in a challenging environment and (expect) slower revenue growth in the near term, we remain confident that AI will help us sustain growth in revenue and profit in the long run," said co-founder and CEO Robin Li in a call to analysts.
The company, China's largest search engine provider, still generates the majority of its revenue from online ad sales, which are under pressure due to slower Chinese economic growth.
It reported on Thursday revenue of 31.51 billion yuan ($4.37 billion) for the three months ended March 31, compared to analysts' average estimate of 31.21 billion yuan as per LSEG data.
"The weak micro economy contributes to the softness of our ad business," Li said.
"Our advertisers come from a wide range of industries with the majority being SME (small and medium-sized enterprises). This means our advertising revenue is highly sensitive to the micro environment."
Baidu's U.S.-listed shares were down 4.8% on the U.S. market opening
During the earnings call on Thursday, Li said daily usage of Ernie by cloud clients had reached 200 million, up from 50 million in the last quarter of 2023.
AI-related revenue contributed 6.9% of the total reported by the cloud business, which rose by 12% to 4.7 billion yuan.
Last month, the company said its AI chatbot Ernie Bot had garnered more than 200 million users, roughly doubling since the company's last update in December.
Baidu started charging users 59.9 yuan per month in November and also seeks to use AI to augment its online search and cloud computing services.
The company's online marketing revenue increased by 3% to 17 billion yuan for the quarter.
In addition to AI, Baidu's diversification efforts away from online search also involve ramping up its autonomous driving business.
Baidu this week announced the launch of a new version of its robotaxi service, the sixth generation, in Wuhan. CEO Li reiterated that the firm aims to achieve profitability next year with its autonomous vehicle business.
The company reported adjusted net income of 7 billion yuan for the quarter, beating the analysts' average estimate of 5.57 billion yuan, according to LSEG data.
